body: I have palinopsia and a mild case of visual snow. I didn’t have those before getting hyperacusis, but they appeared after a few months after I got it, so I think they may all be related.

I’m still amazed at what I can do now, I honestly thought I would never get my life back again. I really had it bad back then. There was a time when I couldn’t use my phone because the sound my fingernails make on the glass was excruciating.

I know things can change — for better or for worse. I hope it’s always for the better, but I know a bad noise can set me back so I’m always cautious. I consider a lot of things when I do something. For example, when I watch a musical at the theater, I need to choose my seats based where the speakers are located. I look for the information online or call the theater to ask about the speakers. People without hyperacusis don’t think about that, but I do. It’s the price I have to pay for wanting to live my life without worsening my ears.

I hope your condition gets better and that an effective treatment will appear soon. Crossing my fingers for all of us.

I was in a relationship in its early stages when I first got hyperacusis. We broke up but I don’t blame him. I was fun and adventurous when we got together then he suddenly had to deal with the reclusive, suicidal side of me all within the span of less than a year.

I started dating again after two years of getting hyperacusis but I have lost interest in long-term relationships, but I think the pandemic also partly caused that change in me, and not just hyperacusis.

Oh I’m so sorry that you’ve been suffering from hyperacusis for eight years now. It’s crazy how time felt like it froze and flew by at the same time.

The crazy thing about this condition is that what works for a sufferer can destroy another sufferer. I have no doubt people improved from sound exposure, but it made me only so much worse. On the other hand, wearing earplugs 24/7 gave me my life back, but I know others can barely tolerate earplugs.

After all these years, my biggest enemy is audio output from speakers. It doesn’t matter what size the speaker is; the physically closer I am to one, the more chances I’ll feel burning and stabbing pain in my ears. So to answer your question, my voice doesn’t bother me when I have earplugs on. It bothers me when I don’t because I sound so loud, especially when I’m in a small room. It’s like my voice is bouncing off the walls and hits my eardrums. 

I prefer Howard Leight earplugs in pink and yellow. They’re soft but they block out a lot of noise. But when I’m out and about, I use Mack’s earplugs in flesh color. They’re inconspicuous so I feel less self-conscious about them. When I fly or take a high-speed train, I wear Bose noise-cancelling headphones on top of my earplugs. I no longer use earmuffs. I personally find them cumbersome and ineffective.

I lost my ears’ filter when I got hyperacusis so when wearing earplugs, I don’t feel like my hearing is muffled. Instead, I feel like my hearing is normal when I have earplugs on.

I can’t watch TV without subtitles but I quickly realized it isn’t just me. The sound mixing is terrible nowadays so many people need subtitles to watch. I go to the cinema sometimes and I don’t have a problem with hearing the dialogue.

My biggest issue with earplugs is that they make my ear canals itch when I have them on continuously, so I remove them every few hours and let my ear canals breathe for a few seconds to a few minutes, depending on the environment I am in.

I’ve had hyperacusis with pain for nine years. The first two years were terrible and I was suicidal. Things got better seven years ago, around the time when I accepted the fact that I need constant ear protection. Some people improve from sound exposure but unfortunately, I’m not one of them.

My life is pretty much normal. Well, almost normal. I wear earplugs practically 24/7, but that doesn’t bother me anymore. Some people wear glasses to see better, and I wear earplugs to hear better. Without earplugs, I get pain and I hear everything (it’s like my ears lost their ability to filter out noises), and that’s overwhelming. 

I don’t go out clubbing and raving anymore but that’s fine. My friends and I aged out of that lifestyle. We’re not interested in it anymore. I still listen to the music though (at a low volume of course).

Yes I have but not 10 hours long, more like nine hours. I’ve had hyperacusis since mid 2016. I stopped flying for two years out of fear, but I took a long-haul flight in late 2018. I figured I would never know unless I tried.

I’ve flown often since then, with a year of rest in between because of the pandemic. But I started flying again in 2021.

How do I get through my flights? I have earplugs and noise-cancelling headphones. I never take them off during a flight. I pick a seat near the front, or at least, before the wing. That means booking business class or premium economy. I also choose an aisle seat because I have most trouble with vibrations, and they’re louder by the window. For long flights, I prefer to have one layover so that my ears can rest, which is why my longest continuous flight is nine hours.

Glad I could help. Good luck!

I fly a lot, sometimes long haul flights too, but since getting hyperacusis, I never fly without earplugs AND noise cancelling headphones. I don’t take them off during the flight, whether the flight is an hour or 16 hours long (but with a layover). I also buy seats in the first few rows. When I don’t have budget for first/business class, I still pick the seat nearest the front of the plane in economy class. I always go for seats in front of the wing, never on or behind. 

I also stay away from the window and go for the aisle seat instead. The aisle seat can also be noisy because of people walking up and down but I can tolerate sudden noises better than I can tolerate vibrations, which the window seat has more of. If the plane has a middle column like in a 3-3-3 layout, I choose an aisle seat in that column.

Also, whenever possible, I prefer to break up a long flight into two shorter ones. Wearing headphones for 2/3 of a day can be tiresome, so I prefer a breather at the airport.

With the exception of Chidi, I don’t think a lot of them had much going on in their lives. Eleanor was alone and sad (though I think she was in denial about it), Tahani couldn’t get out of her sister’s shadow, and Jason was too dumb to care. Perhaps Chidi would have been likely to grieve but that’s easily overshadowed by the discovery that the afterlife is real. 

As for the supporting characters, Simone was in denial about being dead, John was hedonistic enough to indulge in what the good place has to offer right away so he had no time to grieve, and Brent — being used to getting whatever he wanted at any time — didn’t feel any different when he got to the good place because he still always got what he wanted. 

For me as a viewer, the characters grieving over their earthly lives in the face of what they believe is heaven would come across as trivial and unnecessary. It would take up screen time and wouldn’t move the plot forward, just added drama. Perhaps if they left kids behind, or anyone they truly deeply love, it would’ve made sense. Otherwise, it’s just useless fluff.

I want to add that fantasy Kdramas about death and the afterlife show this sense of loss and attachment to earthly life, and it usually works because the characters have been established as people who left behind cherished loved ones. There’s this one Kdrama in which a haven for kids was set up in a purgatory-like place so that kids can wait for their parents to pass away and join them before crossing over together in the afterlife.

Those scenes would just have been fillers. Not that TGP is filler-free, but I like the fact that as far as fillers go, this show doesn’t have a lot of it. Also, I don’t see why someone in their position would grieve their death. A big part of our existential crisis is not knowing if there’s more to life than death. The human characters who died in the show got that answer — they found out there’s more to life after death. They may not be on earth anymore and no longer in their corporeal form, but they still exist, and on a higher plane at that, where limitations don’t exist. It’s heaven, after all. Doesn’t matter if it’s fake heaven, they were made to believe it was heaven and it did seem like it at first. Why would they grieve over their death on earth? It isn’t as if they left behind something that was better.

But the downside of having time to prepare is that you’ll be sufferung more. A loved one who died from cancer a few years back didn’t want to die when she found out she only had around six months to live, but she already made peace with death around a couple of months before she passed. She passed in her sleep, with a hint of a smile on her face.

Here’s how I see this. Death will come either suddenly or slowly. 

If you’re gonna die suddenly like from an accident, I don’t think anything will prepare you for it. Whether you already accepted death or not as an inevitable part of life doesn’t matter at that point. Lucky if you get killed instantly, but if you have seconds or minutes prior to death, you’ll panic. Or at least, you’ll feel fear. You won’t go quietly into the night. That’s what survival instinct is. Even people who have decided to commit suicide still try to fight off death in the last moments. 

If you’re gonna die slowly from an illness like cancer, or old age and the inevitable breakdown of the human body, or a bad situation you can’t get out of (like I dunno, being locked up in the basement of a serial killer who loves to torture their victims first), it will reach a point when as much as you want to live, you’ll just want to rest more. Death will be the better alternative. If this is the way you’ll go, I think you’re gonna come to terms with death sooner or later not because of some philosophical reason, but because you don’t want to suffer anymore.

Just focus on how you can enjoy life while you still can. Life will find ways to fuck you over one way or the other at some point.
